articles.title: China evacuates one million from homes as massive storm arrives
articles.summary: Typhoon Dolphin has made landfall, bringing strong winds and heavy rain across eastern China including Shanghai.
articles.full_text:
Figure caption, 
Watch: Lorry overturns as typhoon hits China By Kelly Ng 
- Published 10 August 2026, 02:44 BST Updated 08:23 BST 
Chinese authorities have evacuated more than a million people from their homes in eastern China including the financial capital Shanghai, as Typhoon Dolphin made landfall. 
The typhoon brought heavy rain and halted transportation across the region. Nearly 1,000 flights were cancelled in Shanghai alone on Monday. 
While authorities have downgraded Dolphin to a tropical storm, they continue to warn of torrential rains, severe flooding and the risk of landslides through to Wednesday as the storm moves north. 
Chinese authorities had earlier issued their highest-level red alert for Dolphin, which is the strongest storm to hit China this year. 
It packed maximum wind speeds of 150km/h (94mph) when it first slammed into Yuhuan in the Zhejiang province at 17:30 (09:30 GMT) on Sunday before making a second landfall in the city of Wenzhou about an hour later, meteorological authorities said. 
Heavy rain was forecast on Monday for the provinces of Shandong, Henan, Hubei, Anhui, Jiangsu, Zhejiang and the city of Shanghai. 
Image source, Reuters Image caption, 
Typhoon Dolphin made landfall in eastern China on Sunday evening 
Image source, Getty Images Image caption, 
Residents wade through flooded streets in Shanghai 
Governments have urged people to avoid outdoor activities, while several top tourist attractions remain closed, including parts of Disneyland and Legoland, and several viewing platforms along the Bund in Shanghai. 
Footage on state media show ground-floor businesses flooded in the former French Concession in Shanghai, an area popular with tourists, and people wading through ankle-deep waters. 
Several state media outlets have reported that a nine-year-old boy from Wenling, Zhejiang is missing after being swept into the sea. Chinese officials have not reported any casualties. 
Parts of Zhejiang could receive 250mm to 500mm of rain over the next few days, forecasters say. 
Authorities in Hangzhou, Zhejiang's capital city, have waived parking fees in all public spaces for drivers seeking shelter amid the strong winds and floodwaters. 
Elsewhere in the province, Wenzhou authorities have relocated some 900,000 residents and opened more than 1,000 emergency shelters, while about 390,000 people have been evacuated from their homes in the city of Taizhou. 
In the coastal province of Fujian, maritime authorities have suspended dozens of passenger ferry routes and halted more than 100 offshore construction projects. 
The storm moved over a long distance of 6,000km before making landfall, suggesting a lifespan of more than three times that of an average typhoon, according to China's state broadcaster CCTV. 
It also has a massive circulation size and intense rainfall capacity, CCTV reported. 
Image source, Reuters Image caption, 
The typhoon has disrupted transportation services 
Misinformation around the storm has apparently spread rapidly on the Chinese internet, with state media reporting that two people have been detained for distributing such content. 
One of them, a 60-year-old man, created a fake video with AI that claimed someone in Shanghai had fallen from a building during the storm. 
Another man, 32, had re-edited storm footage posted by other social media users in a way that was deemed as misleading. 
Dolphin brought torrential rains to the Philippines, parts of northern Taiwan and Japan's Okinawa island before bearing down on China. 
- 
AI or real? BBC analyses viral China disaster videos 
- Published 5 days ago 
Image source, Getty Images Image caption, 
More than 7,000 people are sheltering at evacuation centres nationwide in the Philippines 
Eight people have died in the Philippines because of heavy monsoon rains brought on by Dolphin and storms earlier in the week, says the Office of Civil Defence. More than 7,000 people are sheltering at evacuation centres nationwide. 
In Okinawa in Japan, five elderly people suffered non-life-threatening injuries, according to the prefectural government. 
Three of them fell because of the strong winds, it said. 
Meanwhile in Hong Kong, weather observatory posted a record high temperature of 36.9C on Sunday as the typhoon swept warm air over the city. 
Typhoon season in the western Pacific typically occurs between May and October, when typhoons are considered more commonplace. 
This year is a strong El Niño year, which experts say means typhoons can grow to be more intense.

articles.title: Trump imposes 15% tariff on key chip material to counter China
articles.summary: The move  aims to protect US firms as they face increasing competition from China's chip industry.
articles.full_text:
Image source, VCG via Getty Images Image caption, 
China is the world's biggest producer of polysilicon, a key material used in making chips and solar panels By Osmond Chia Business reporter 
- Published 7 August 2026 
US President Donald Trump signed an executive order on Thursday that imposes a 15% tariff on imported products made from polysilicon, a crucial material used in semiconductors and solar panels. 
The order also set minimum import prices on polysilicon and related products. It comes after a national security investigation into the production of the material overseas. 
The move is intended to help protect US manufacturers as they face increasing competition from China's chip industry - a key source of friction between the world's two largest economies. 
The Chinese embassy in Washington said the move "seriously disrupts" trade between the two countries and Beijing will act to protect its companies. 
Washington is "abusing state power to go after Chinese businesses," the embassy said, adding that protectionism will not make the US more competitive. 
Trump said in the order , external that he had accepted recommendations by Secretary of Commerce Howard Lutnick to set minimum import prices as well as a 15% tariff on polysilicon and related imports. 
The measures are due to take effect in December. 
The US will also offer incentives to boost domestic production, it added. 
For decades, the US has allowed "foreign firms to weaken United States producers in the polysilicon sector," said Trump, who has long advocated for the use of tariffs to protect American jobs and boost the economy. 
The material is critical in military equipment and electronics, yet imports have led to the US' share of global polysilicon production to fall from 50% in 2005 to less than 2% in 2024, Trump said. 
China holds a near monopoly on the production of polysilicon. 
The order is likely to benefit Hemlock Semiconductor and Wacker Chemie, which are the main producers of the material in the US. 
The production of computer chips is central to the race between the US and China to develop artificial intelligence (AI). Washington and Beijing have also been locked in a tit-for-tat tariffs war , which has been on hold since May 2025. 
Analysts quoted by Chinese state media outlet Global Times said the new tariff marks the latest escalation in Washington's efforts to limit China's role in critical technology supply chains. 
The move follows other US restrictions on the imports of drones, humanoid robots and other tech products from China. 
China announced a range of countermeasures this week, including tighter export controls on drones. Beijing also launched a national security review into imported printers and copiers.

articles.title: Typhoon Dolphin batters Japan's Okinawa before bearing down on China
articles.summary: The storm has cut power to at least 44,000 buildings and injured five people on the Japanese island.
articles.full_text:
Image source, X/Reuters Image caption, 
The islands of Amami and Okinawa are the parts of Japan most affected by the typhoon By Jack Burgess 
- Published 8 August 2026 
Typhoon Dolphin has cut power to at least 44,000 buildings and injured at least five people after hitting Japan's Okinawa island on Saturday. 
Flights to and from Okinawa's main airport - Naha International Airport - were cancelled as it closed on Friday as the storm arrived. 
The storm had maximum wind speeds of 162km/h (101mph) on Saturday and has been categorised as a "very strong" typhoon by the Japan Meteorological Agency, which warned of high waves, storm surges and lightning strikes. 
Dolphin is expected to make landfall on China's eastern coast late on Sunday or early on Monday. Authorities there have shut ports and schools ahead of its arrival. 
The main areas in Japan affected by the typhoon are the islands of Okinawa and Amami in the far south-west of the country. 
Five elderly people suffered non-life-threatening injuries, according to the Okinawan prefectural government. Three of them fell because of the strong winds, it said. 
Japan's national broadcaster NHK reports numerous accounts of trees being toppled by strong winds throughout Nago city in Okinawa, while a car was found overturned and leaking oil in a parking lot. 
Image source, Reuters Image caption, 
Satellite imagery showing Typhoon Dolphin approaching Japan's Okinawa during the week 
In China, Zhejiang's Ningbo Lishe International Airport said it would stop its operations from 23:30 local time on Saturday (15:30 GMT) and suspend all flights on Sunday. 
A coastal typhoon alert in Zhejiang has been raised to its highest level, and port and ferry services have been halted in the Chinese province. 
In Hong Kong, its weather observatory posted a record high temperature of 36.9C on Sunday as Typhoon Dolphin swept warm air over the city. 
Typhoon season in the western Pacific typically occurs between May and October, when typhoons are considered more commonplace. This year is a strong El Niño year , which experts say means typhoons can grow to be more intense. 
In an average year of 25 cyclones reaching tropical storm strength in the region, around three usually make landfall in Japan, according to the country's meteorological agency. 
Some of these will be strong enough to be classified as typhoons – as was the case with Dolphin. 
A typhoon is the term used for storms that form in the north-west Pacific, whereas a hurricane is the term used for storms that form in the Atlantic or eastern Pacific. 
Image source, Japan Meteorological Agency Image caption, 
The typhoon is expected to make landfall on China's eastern coast late on Sunday or early on Monday

articles.title: He's been frozen on Everest for 30 years, now 'Green Boots' may finally be coming home
articles.summary: For decades, an Indian man's lime shoes have been a grim trail marker for many climbing the world's highest peak.
articles.full_text:
Image source, Family handout Image caption, 
Dorje Morup was a keen mountaineer and had climbed many peaks, including Stok Kangri, the highest peak in the Ladakh mountain range By Jehangir Ali BBC News Hindi ,  Reporting from Skurbuchan, Ladakh 
- Published 8 August 2026 
For 30 years, a dead body known as "Green Boots" has been lying in the snow, nestled under an overhanging rock, not far from Mount Everest's summit. 
The lime mountaineering boots worn by an Indian climber who died in 1996 have been a grim trail marker for many climbers on their way up the world's highest peak ever since. 
Now India is looking for a specialist high-altitude recovery team to undertake a complex and risky mission to retrieve what they say is Dorje Morup's body – arguably the most famous of the hundreds whose bodies have been left frozen on the mountain. 
Warning: This story contains a picture of a dead body. 
They hope they are on the cusp of returning his remains to friends and family who never gave up hope he'd come home. 
"On some days, before I went to sleep, I would think that there'd be a knock on the door tonight and that when I opened, he would be there," Morup's wife told the BBC. 
"When he comes home, I will ask him: 'Where were you all these years?'" 
Disaster struck on descent 
Image source, Supplied Image caption, 
The body of Indian climber Dorje Morup who died 30 years ago wearing his green mountaineering boots has become a grim marker along the road to Everest's summit 
The night before he left to be part of a historic Indian expedition on Everest, Morup sat with his wife at his home in Ladakh, an Indian-administered territory in another part of the Himalayas. 
He made her a promise: that he would come back a hero and make his country proud. 
"He asked me to take care of the kids and come to the airport to greet him on his return," Konchak Yangskit told the BBC at her home. 
A lance naik, or lance corporal, in the Indo Tibetan Border Police (ITBP), the force guarding much of India's border with China, 48-year-old Morup was no stranger to Himalayan trekking. 
But Yangskit says she had a strange sense of foreboding that night: "I wondered if I was ever going to see him again." 
Morup was one of six climbers on the ITBP expedition attempting to reach the top of Everest – which lies on the border between Nepal and the Chinese-governed territory of Tibet. 
Most climbers choose to ascend from the Nepalese side, but Morup's crew wanted to write their names into the history books as the first Indian expedition to do it from the treacherous Chinese side. 
Image caption, 
Morup's wife, Yangskit, says because she never saw his body, she found it difficult to believe he was dead 
Three out of six members of the expedition turned back due to a snowstorm, but Morup and two others - Tsewang Smanla and Tsewang Paljor – kept struggling, all the way up to the 8,849m summit. 
Disaster, a blizzard, struck as they descended and killed all three. 
Like many of the more than 300 people who have died in the Everest region since records began a century ago, their bodies remain on the mountain. 
Two have never been found, but the third body - that of "Green Boots" - has been lying frozen in the snow for three decades at an altitude of 8,500 metres. 
For years, it was assumed that "Green Boots" was another member of the expedition, Tsewang Paljor. 
But testimony from surviving members of the 1996 expedition and the location of the last radio contact with the climbers have now led authorities to believe the remains belong to Morup. 
Image source, Family handout Image caption, 
Morup's family is proud to show the certificate issued by the Chinese government confirming he had successfully reached the top of Everest 
An ITBP official, speaking anonymously because he is not authorised to speak to the media, told BBC News Hindi that Morup's clothes and climbing gear helped officials identify the body in recent years. 
Since then, they've been plotting how to get their comrade home so they can confirm his identity beyond doubt through DNA testing and offer his family a semblance of closure. 
"We never forgot him. It was only a matter of time," the ITBP official said. 
How difficult will it be to recover the body? 
Retrieving those who have died on the mountain is a dangerous, gruelling task, and, up until the past decade, very rare. 
Many of the bodies, like Morup's, are in what climbers call Everest's death zone – where temperatures can plunge to -40C and oxygen levels are about a third of those at sea level. 
"The weather and snow conditions are going to be crucial," said Tshiring Jangbu Sherpa, a prominent Nepalese mountaineer who has taken part in other recovery missions. 
"The north side has fewer crevasses, but it is riskier. If something bad happens from the Nepalese side, you get quickly evacuated by helicopter. But there is no such system from the Chinese side," he told BBC Hindi. 
Image caption, 
Some of photos of Morup and a few of his belongings have helped his family keep his memory alive 
The Chinese side of the peak – where Green Boots' body is – is steeper and doesn't have the same support structures as the southern slope, which is another complicating factor, Sherpa sources have told BBC News Nepali. 
"It's really tough to get that body down even in popular spring season, let alone the autumn [which has more unpredictable weather]. That's the simple reason it is still there for so many years," mountaineering guide Pemba Ongchu Sherpa said. 
"There would need to be 10 to 12 climbers who are capable of making summits, just to fix [support] ropes to reach that point." 
Green Boots will also have to be physically carried down to an altitude where it can be collected by a helicopter, or possibly yaks, and transported back to an airport – a job which also requires huge manpower. 
Sherpas say bodies shrouded in iced-up climbing gear often weigh several times the average man and are frequently frozen into awkward positions, making bringing them down the challenging terrain even more treacherous. The remains may also begin defrosting and decomposing once they reach lower altitudes. 
The start of the descent with the body would be the most difficult, Indian climber Kuntal Joisher told BBC Nepali. 
"It's going to be very, very risky endeavour. It's extremely steep ground with lots of rock. Logistically, this [first] 1000m is going to be a humungous challenge." 
"The main thing is to not put Sherpa lives at risk for a dead body." 
All of this makes for a hugely expensive recovery mission – experts say even the most straightforward ones cost between $40,000 and $80,000, a sum beyond the means of most families. 
It is more common for local teams to move people who have died out of view on the mountain: like explorer Francys Arsentiev, dubbed the Sleeping Beauty of Everest, who in 2007 was moved to a more private final resting place on Everest almost a decade after she died. 
But the ITBP – which is funding the recovery operation – wants Morup's body to be returned by September, and is looking for mountain rescue Sherpa groups who could do the job. 
Once returned to India, the body will undergo DNA testing and, if confirmed to be Morup, his remains will be given back to his family. 
'My heart refused to believe he had died' 
For years, Morup's family back in Ladakh have struggled to come to terms with his disappearance. 
Now around 75, Yangskit struggles to recall even the day she was married. But the days after the tragedy remain etched in her mind. 
"I only knew there was a storm on the mountain. Even though we organised cremation prayers at home, my heart refused to believe he had died," she says with tears rolling down her face. 
"I didn't see his dead body, so it was difficult for me to believe it." 
Image caption, 
Morup's family remains cautious about what the body being returned will mean for them 
Image caption, 
Morup's eldest son, Punchok Dorjai, looks up at a framed photo of his father 
All that remains of Morup today are his medals and trophies, a couple of old photos from his mountain adventures – and, most importantly, a certificate from the Chinese government which states that at 17:30 on 10 May 1996, Morup reached the top of Everest. 
If the recovery mission is successful, Morup's son Punchok Dorjai told the BBC that the family would hold a funeral for him near the Martyrs Park in Ladakh's capital Leh. 
"My father gave his life for the country and he should be remembered as a martyr," Dorjai said, adding that his teammates who perished deserve the same title. 
The family will also proudly save a symbol of Morup's legacy at their home, to go alongside his summit certification, he said: "We are planning to keep the Green Boots." 
Additional reporting by Pradeep Bashyal, BBC News Nepali

articles.title: Weather tracker: Europe breaks more heat records as temperatures soar
articles.summary: Drought and wildfires intensify across continent, while tropical storms bring heavy rain and disruption to east AsiaHigh pressure has dominated central and eastern Europe in early August, breaking temperature records  across the region. Austria recorded a high of 41.2C (106.2F), while Slovakia reached 42.2C. Hungary hit a peak of 41.8C, surpassing a record set in 1905, while overnight temperatures remained above 28C in some areas, marking it as a tropical night.The extreme temperatures have been driven by a heat dome beneath the high-pressure system, which traps warm air close to the surface. Drought and wildfires intensify across continent, while tropical storms bring heavy rain and disruption to east Asia 
High pressure has dominated central and eastern Europe in early August, breaking temperature records across the region. Austria recorded a high of 41.2C (106.2F), while Slovakia reached 42.2C. Hungary hit a peak of 41.8C, surpassing a record set in 1905, while overnight temperatures remained above 28C in some areas, marking it as a tropical night. 
The extreme temperatures have been driven by a heat dome beneath the high-pressure system, which traps warm air close to the surface. 
The prolonged heat has dried out soil and vegetation, creating conditions conducive to the spread of wildfires. Fires have burned across Italy, France, Serbia and Bulgaria, damaging forests and forcing residents to evacuate. 
Water levels in the Danube, which flows through much of the affected region, have fallen to an all-time low . The receding river has exposed archaeological remains and wartime wreckage , including woolly mammoth bones, second world war ships and remains associated with the Roman-era Constantine’s Bridge. 
Low water levels have also affected energy production, reducing the efficiency of nuclear power plants in Slovakia and Serbia and forcing Hungary to shut down a plant because there was insufficient water for cooling. 
Meanwhile, a buoy in the Mediterranean recorded a sea-surface temperature of 33C. If verified, it would be the highest recorded in the region. 
In eastern Asia, Typhoon Dolphin made landfall in China on Sunday. The national observatory had issued a red alert for the storm – the highest level – for prolonged heavy rainfall , high wind speeds and extensive damage. Dolphin has since weakened to a tropical storm. 
Japan is braced for Typhoon Chan-hom, just days after Dolphin swept through northern Okinawa and the Amami islands. Chan-hom is expected to make landfall near the coast of Tohoku between Tuesday and Wednesday, with up to 80mph (129km/h) gusts and an atmospheric pressure of 985 hPa. 
A third system, Peilou, formed on Sunday in the western Pacific. Although it is not expected to make landfall in the Philippines , it is likely to strengthen the south-west monsoon, bringing further rain across the country. Other typhoons this year have intensified the monsoon, which has killed six people and displaced more than 380,000.

Typhoon Dolphin: more than a million people evacuated in China as record rainfall dumped on Shanghai
Authorities warn that days of intense rain could trigger widespread flooding and landslides as storm moves north and further inland 
More than a million people were moved to safety across eastern China by Sunday evening as powerful Typhoon Dolphin made landfall amid fears torrential rain would cause flooding and landslides. 
Wenzhou, a coastal city in Zhejiang province, said it relocated more than 900,000 people and opened more than 1,500 emergency shelters. In neighbouring Fujian, 98,900 people were moved from high-risk areas. Hong Kong records hottest day ever as Typhoon Dolphin fuels heatwave 
Read more 
In Shanghai, 215,600 people were moved from areas considered at risk by Sunday evening, substantially higher than an earlier figure of 30,300. 
A weather station in central Shanghai recorded nearly 313mm of rain in the 24 hours to 7am on Monday, its highest 24-hour rainfall in more than 150 years of records. Another station in the city recorded nearly 400mm. The hashtag “Shanghai turns into the sea” began trending on the Chinese social media platform Weibo, as videos circulated showing streets flooded around the Wukang Mansion, one of the city’s best-known tourist landmarks. 
The average rainfall recorded across Zhejiang from Friday evening to Monday morning reached 173mm, reportedly surpassing the levels seen during previous major typhoons including Lekima and Bavi. 
Dolphin weakened rapidly to a tropical storm by 5am on Monday. But as the storm continued to move northwards and farther inland, heavy rain was forecast across large parts of eastern and central China , extending north into Shandong and affecting Henan, Hubei, Anhui, Jiangsu, Zhejiang and Shanghai. 
Authorities maintained an orange alert for heavy rain and warned that days of intense rain could trigger widespread flooding and landslides through Wednesday, urging people to stay indoors during the heavy downpours. Forecasters in China predicted some areas could see 200-400mm (7.9–15.7 inches) of rainfall over the coming days. 
View image in fullscreen 
A temporary shelter in Hangzhou, where thousands of people were evacuated because of Typhoon Dolphin. Photograph: VCG/Getty Images 
The storm forced Shanghai’s two airports to cancel more than 1,300 flights. Public transport services, including many local trains, have been suspended in the financial hub. 
Zhejiang’s Ningbo international airport, about 150km south of Shanghai, will resume flight operations from midday (0400 GMT) on Monday. But the airport warned some journeys may yet be delayed or cancelled. 
Provincial capital Hangzhou resumed subway services on Monday morning, after halting some train operations on Sunday. 
Elsewhere, Dolphin fuelled intense heat over Hong Kong on Sunday, pushing the city to its highest ever temperature of 36.9C . The extremely hot weather was expected to continue into Tuesday, officials said. 
In Taiwan, ferry services were suspended and more than 180 flights were cancelled as the storm brought downpours and strong winds on Sunday. 
Dolphin earlier swept through Japan’s southern Okinawa prefecture, injuring six people and ⁠cutting power to more than 50,000 buildings. 
In the Philippines, the typhoon did not make landfall in the country’s north but intensified the seasonal monsoon rains, which flooded many areas of the main northern Luzon region, including around Manila. 
Scientists say global warming has made extreme weather more likely, including more powerful typhoons.

People watch huge waves hit a waterfront in Sanmen county, Zhejiang province, as Typhoon Dolphin approaches Photograph: cnsphoto/Reuters 
Typhoon Dolphin makes landfall in China as its strongest storm this year
Tropical cyclone brings torrential rain and high winds to east coast after hitting Japan’s southern Okinawa province 
Typhoon Dolphin, the most powerful tropical cyclone to hit China this year, has made landfall on the country’s east coast, bringing torrential rain and strong ⁠winds and triggering warnings ​of flooding and landslides. 
The storm has already swept through Japan’s southern Okinawa prefecture, injuring six people and cutting power to more than 50,000 buildings. 
Dolphin made landfall near Yuhuan in Zhejiang province at about ⁠5:30pm (0930 GMT) on Sunday, China’s meteorological authorities said. It brought maximum sustained winds of 94mph (151 km/h) near its centre at landfall, equivalent to a category 1 hurricane on the Saffir-Simpson scale. 
In addition to evacuating at least 30,300 people, Shanghai has cancelled about 1,500 flights, according to the flight-tracking data provider VariFlight. 
View image in fullscreen 
A struggles against high winds and driving rain in Dongsha, Zhejiang province, as Typhoon Dolphin makes landfall. Photograph: Huang Zongzhi/Xinhua/AP Hong Kong records hottest day ever as Typhoon Dolphin fuels heatwave 
Read more 
Authorities moved offshore ⁠workers to safety, ordered vessels back to port and increased checks at reservoirs, mountain streams, landslide-prone areas, construction sites and tourist locations. 
Torrential ​rain is forecast for Monday across Zhejiang, Shanghai, northern Fujian, ‌north-eastern Jiangxi, central and southern Anhui, and ‌much of Jiangsu. Parts of central and eastern Zhejiang could receive 250-500 mm (10-20 inches) of rain, according to forecasters. 
Dolphin was forecast to track ‌westward before slowing over central and south-western China and gradually losing strength, the chief forecaster at the National Meteorological Centre, Wang Haiping, told the state broadcaster CCTV. 
That could prolong heavy rain and increase the risk of flooding and landslides, especially in mountainous areas and along smaller rivers. 
1:12 
Typhoon Dolphin batters parts of east and south-east Asia – video 
Transport was widely disrupted across the east of the country and more than a million people were evacuated from their homes. 
A 42-year-old tourist from Guangdong, surnamed Chen, said he had been stranded in Shanghai ‌after his family’s flight, scheduled to depart on Sunday, was cancelled. 
He said the family had been rebooked on a flight at 10pm on Monday, although they were unsure whether it would be able ​to take off. 
“To us Guangdong people, this typhoon is as ordinary as having a meal and feeling the wind. It’s just part of everyday life,” he said, adding that the storm did not appear particularly strong by the standards of China’s southern coast. 
View image in fullscreen 
A woman wades through floodwater in Shanghai. Photograph: cnsphoto/Reuters 
In neighbouring Zhejiang province, the city of Wenzhou relocated more than 900,000 people and opened more than 1,000 emergency shelters. In Fujian province, authorities evacuated 98,900 people from high-risk areas, according to Xinhua. 
Fujian maritime authorities ​said 55 coastal passenger ferry routes had been suspended, ​all 115 offshore construction projects halted and 290 construction ​vessels moved to sheltered waters. 
The water resources ministry said the Qiantang, Yong, Jiao and Shuiyang rivers could experience major ​flooding, while smaller rivers in the ‌hardest-hit areas could rise above ​warning levels. 
Authorities issued an alert for the risk of geological disasters in parts of Zhejiang. Residents in areas covered by a red mountain-torrent warning were told to follow local evacuation orders. 
Shanghai’s Yangshan port had cleared ships from its berths and moved more than 500 small and medium-sized vessels to shelter as Dolphin approached, the city’s maritime safety administration said. 
Scientists say global warming has made extreme weather more likely, including more powerful typhoons.
